The proposed architecture is computationally scalable, data efficient, and adaptable to a variety of degradation patterns. These results demonstrate the potential of combining sequential latent-space policy optimization with generative representation learning to provide a modular and efficient sequential RUL estimation method for challenging industrial scenarios.

title: Cortex: A Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Career-Aligned Learning Paths
abstract: In an era of rapidly evolving professional development, many learners and individuals transitioning careers find it challenging to align their existing skills with the demands of their desired professions. Conventional career guidance systems often rely on rigid keyword matching, which overlooks the semantic nuances of users’ intentions. For instance, a user interested in “interpreting big data” may not explicitly mention “Data Scientist,” causing traditional systems to miss this connection. Furthermore, once a career path is identified, determining an optimal sequence for skill acquisition–while considering prerequisites and dependencies–remains a significant pedagogical challenge that is rarely automated effectively at scale. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Cortex , an AI-based career-aligned learning system that combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), large language models (LLMs), knowledge graphs, and sentence embeddings to semantically match user interests with occupations and generate prerequisite-consistent upskilling paths with inter-skill dependencies and scaffolding. The primary scientific contribution is a novel end-to-end architecture connecting semantic intent understanding, prerequisite-aware skill sequencing via ESCO dependency graphs, and taxonomy-constrained LLM generation. The system leverages the ESCO dataset to map career goals to relevant skills and produce structured learning paths. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating LLMs with a constrained RAG framework and knowledge graph-based dependency modeling can effectively generate prerequisite-aware learning paths for diverse career goals.

title: Explainable Federated Learning for Trustworthy Thoracic Disease Detection Under Non-IID Data Distributions
abstract: Privacy regulations prevent hospitals from sharing patient chest radiographs for collaborative AI training, limiting diagnostic model generalisability. This paper proposes FedXAI-Health, an explainable federated learning framework for multi-label thoracic disease classification across five Non-IID hospital clients using the NIH Chest X-ray 14 dataset with patient-level train/test splits ensuring zero data leakage. Under identical experimental conditions (EfficientNetB0, batch size 512, Adam with weight decay \(10^{-4}\) ), FedAvg achieves Macro-AUC of \(0.8060 \pm 0.0048\) , surpassing the centralised EfficientNetB0 baseline of \(0.7859 \pm 0.0142\) by 2.0% while preserving complete patient data privacy. FedProx achieves \(0.7879 \pm 0.0020\) . Comparison of SHAP and Grad-CAM attribution maps confirms clinically coherent disease-specific localisation. Ablation across five proximal parameter values ( \(\mu \in \{0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0\}\) ) reveals monotonic performance degradation, identifying minimal regularisation as optimal for multi-label medical imaging. Robustness to Non-IID heterogeneity is validated across Dirichlet \(\alpha \in \{0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0\}\) . All results report mean ± std across 3 independent runs. Code: https://github.com/itsuresha/fedxai-health .

title: SentiMatrix: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Encoder-Based Transformers for Multidimensional Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Abstract Transformer-based architectures have established state-of-the-art benchmarks across Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks; however, the computational overhead of full fine-tuning remains a significant barrier to scalable deployment. This paper presents SentiMatrix, a systematic evaluation of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)-based Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) across four sentiment analysis paradigms: Intent-based, Aspect-based, Fine-grained, and Emotion detection, spanning seven benchmark datasets under a consistent three-stage protocol: inference using task-specific pretrained baseline models (i.e., HuggingFace checkpoints previously fine-tuned on the corresponding benchmarks, serving as informed upper-bound references rather than cold-start zero-shot baselines), Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) as a performance upper bound, and LoRA-based adaptation to quantify the efficiency-performance trade-off. Adaptive Low-Rank Adaptation (AdaLoRA) is benchmarked as a direct comparator. LoRA achieves competitive performance while reducing trainable parameters by up to 99.8%, with lower GPU memory usage and training time in most evaluated settings. It achieves 93.28% accuracy on SST-2, 80.74% on combined Laptop+Restaurant ABSA, 67.63% on E-Commerce 5-class, and 93.22% on emotion detection, while closely approaching FFT on E-Commerce 5-class (68.47%). The results demonstrate an effective efficiency-performance trade-off across diverse sentiment analysis tasks. Ablation experiments examine the effects of adaptation strategy, model capacity, and label granularity. The source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ELTE-DSED/senti-matrix .

title: CASE: Contrastive Activation for Class-Sensitive Explanations
abstract: Abstract Saliency methods are widely used to visualize which input features are deemed relevant to a model’s prediction. However, their visual plausibility can obscure critical limitations. In this work, we propose a diagnostic test for class sensitivity: a method’s ability to distinguish between competing class labels on the same input. Through experiments on single-label natural-image classification, we show that many widely used saliency methods produce nearly identical explanations regardless of the class label, calling into question their reliability. We find that class-insensitive behavior persists across multiple convolutional architectures and datasets, suggesting that the failure mode is not tied to a single model family or benchmark. Motivated by these findings, we introduce CASE, a contrastive explanation method that isolates features for the predicted class. We evaluate CASE using the proposed diagnostic and a perturbation-based fidelity test, and show that it produces consistently more class-specific explanations while maintaining competitive fidelity.

title: SPIRAL: A Novel Time Series to Image (TS2I) Transformation Method for Vision-Based Anomaly Detection
abstract: Abstract Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) underpins critical applications in manufacturing, healthcare, finance, and cloud computing. Recently, time series to image (TS2I) transformations have emerged as a promising approach that enables leveraging pretrained vision models for time series analysis. However, the majority of existing TS2I methods were designed for forecasting and classification, and suffer from parameter sensitivity, symmetric redundancy, and quadratic computational complexity. In this study, we introduce SPIRAL, a novel TS2I transformation designed for TSAD. SPIRAL maps time series windows onto a two-arm Archimedean spiral, producing asymmetric representations that preserve temporal locality while eliminating redundancy with linear time complexity with respect to window length. We additionally propose a standardized workflow with ACF-based window selection and point-wise scoring. Extensive evaluation (24,430 experiments) on 23 datasets from the TSB-AD benchmark, comparing SPIRAL against 9 TS2I transformations, 3 vision backbones, and 32 time-domain baselines across 9 metrics, shows that SPIRAL achieves the best average rank among 102 configurations in challenging metrics such as VUS-PR while exhibiting 40% lower training instability than its closest TS2I competitor. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Smendowski/SPIRAL .

title: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent for Outcome Weighted Learning
abstract: Abstract The development of individualized treatment rules in precision medicine seeks to optimize clinical outcomes for patients with varying responses to treatment. This paper focuses on outcome weighted learning, a method for estimating optimal treatment rules that take into account patient-specific characteristics within a weighted classification framework. We introduce a differentially private stochastic gradient descent algorithm within the framework of outcome weighted learning. This approach involves adding Gaussian noise to the gradient at each iteration, thereby ensuring the privacy of sensitive medical data while effectively managing large-scale datasets common in clinical practice. Unlike traditional differential privacy methods, which primarily focus on input-output type data, our approach integrates input-action-reward type data. This incorporation guarantees that both privacy and utility are preserved, with utility measured by the excess value function of the estimated individualized treatment rule. In our analysis, we establish convergence rates for the excess value function under logistic loss function, hinge loss function, and smoothed hinge loss function constructed via the Moreau envelope. These results provide rigorous utility guarantees for differentially private outcome weighted learning in precision medicine. Furthermore, empirical experiments support these theoretical findings and highlight the practical value of smoothing techniques in privacy-preserving learning for precision medicine.

title: CausalCACTUS: A Causally Consistent and Context-Aware Framework for Counterfactual Explanations
abstract: Abstract Counterfactual explanations have been proposed to provide actionable insights for complex black-box classifiers by suggesting “what-if” explanations that alter undesirable prediction outcomes to desired ones. Recent advances have emphasized desirable properties such as causality, plausibility, and contextual alignment; however, existing methods often address these objectives in isolation. In particular, causal counterfactual approaches enforce structural dependencies among features, typically assuming access to a fully specified structural causal model, while context-aware counterfactual frameworks focus on improving alignment with user-defined contextual constraints. As a result, a gap remains between context-aware and causally grounded counterfactual generation, especially in latent-space representations, which can jointly address multiple objectives and improve validity across domains. In this work, we introduce CausalCACTUS, a causally consistent and context-aware counterfactual explanation framework that extends the CACTUS method by integrating automatically learned causal structure into latent-space counterfactual generation using a composite $$\beta $$ -VAE model. CausalCACTUS incorporates a directed acyclic graph learned from data-driven causal discovery to impose causal feasibility constraints, together with a phase-based latent optimization strategy that improves convergence stability and counterfactual validity while preserving user-defined contextual constraints. Our experimental evaluation across five publicly available tabular datasets and multiple baseline models demonstrates that CausalCACTUS achieves improved context alignment and causal consistency metrics while maintaining competitive performance on standard counterfactual metrics, such as validity and proximity. Ablation studies and qualitative examples further illustrate that jointly enforcing context preservation and causal structure leads to more actionable, trustworthy counterfactual explanations that respect user-defined contexts and causal dependencies in real-world scenarios.

title: Joint Representation Learning for Expert Discovery
abstract: The success of community question answering (CQA) platforms is in part dependent on how well questions are matched with the best experts that can effectively answer them in a timely manner. As the complexity of questions on CQA platforms increases, necessitating the collaboration of multiple experts, existing expert-finding methods are inadequate because they are designed to evaluate the suitability of individual experts for specific questions rather than collaborative expertise. This paper introduces a novel approach to identify collaborative teams of experts by employing graph neural networks and kernel pooling techniques, trained end-to-end. Our approach not only predicts potential individual experts but also forms teams that collectively enhance the answer quality. Through extensive experiments on real-life datasets, we show our proposed model is able to (1) find more qualified experts for new questions by at least \(4.4\%\) and \(6.7\%\) superior ranks in terms of ranking metrics NDCG and MAP , respectively, compared to the best expert finding baselines; (2) form a collaborative team of experts with \(4.7\%\) higher skill coverage than collaborative expert finding baselines.

title: FedHybrid-ViT: A Federated-Hybrid Framework for Generalizable Deepfake Detection on Heterogeneous Data
abstract: The rapid advancement of deep generative models has significantly increased the realism and accessibility of deepfake media, posing serious threats to digital integrity, public trust, and information security. Although recent deepfake detection methods report high accuracy on benchmark datasets, their performance often degrades under real-world conditions due to domain shift and data heterogeneity. Centralized models tend to overfit to dataset-specific artifacts and fail to generalize across diverse data sources, while federated learning (FL) approaches, although privacy-preserving, suffer from unstable convergence when trained on non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) client data. To address these challenges, we propose FedHybrid-ViT, a privacy-aware deepfake detection framework that integrates a dual-stream Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) within a federated learning setting. The CNN branch captures local high-frequency artifacts such as blending inconsistencies and compression traces, whereas the ViT branch models global semantic relationships across facial regions. The complementary features are fused to enable robust multi-scale representation learning. The framework is trained using a collaborative federated optimization protocol, allowing decentralized model updates without sharing raw data and thereby reducing the need for centralized raw data sharing. We evaluate the proposed approach on a heterogeneous multi-source dataset constructed from publicly available deepfake benchmarks under both independent and non-IID distribution settings. Experimental results demonstrate that FedHybrid-ViT consistently outperforms standalone CNN and ViT models as well as standard federated baselines. The proposed method achieves an AUC of 0.925 and maintains stable performance across highly heterogeneous conditions, indicating improved robustness under heterogeneous source distributions. These results highlight the effectiveness of combining hybrid architectures with federated learning for scalable and robust deepfake detection, offering a promising approach for distributed deepfake detection scenarios.

title: Knockoff-Guided Compressive Sensing: A Statistical Machine Learning Framework for Support-Assured Signal Recovery
abstract: Compressive sensing (CS) is a technique used to recover signals from incomplete or compressed measurements, enabling efficient signal reconstruction. However, commonly used methods like \(\ell _1\) -based approaches (e.g., LASSO) do not directly control the rate of false discoveries when selecting the correct signal components, especially in the presence of correlations between measurements. To address this, we propose KnockoffCS , a novel framework that incorporates a knockoff-guided mechanism for support selection. This framework not only controls the false discovery rate (FDR)-a statistical measure to limit false positives-but also employs a separate estimation stage to improve signal recovery. Our theoretical analysis shows that by enforcing FDR control, KnockoffCS can reliably identify the correct components and reconstruct signals, even under conditions that are weaker than those typically required by \(\ell _1\) methods, while maintaining high accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of KnockoffCS over existing baselines. In synthetic simulations, KnockoffCS significantly improves support recovery (up to \(3.9\times \) improvement in F1 score) and reduces reconstruction errors. On real-world datasets, KnockoffCS achieves strong downstream predictive performance, surpassing existing CS methods in 71.4% of evaluated modelâ€“dataset combinations, ranking in the top two among CS methods (compared to the compressed baseline, gains are dataset/predictor-dependent). However, performance varies depending on the dataset and predictor, with certain datasets where compressed signal baselines remain competitive. These results highlight KnockoffCS as an effective and strong competitive alternative that integrates statistical guarantees into compressive sensing, offering both theoretical reliability and strong empirical results.

title: Large Language Model Guided Series Saliency Module for Accurate and Interpretable Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Time series data analysis is an essential task in numerous critical applications, such as air quality assessment and stock price prediction, where the goal is to extract underlying patterns and predict future values. Despite the recent strong performance of deep models in multivariate time series forecasting, their failure to utilize essential trend information may hinder their effectiveness in filtering out anomalous patterns such as sawtooth shapes and spikes, thereby negatively affecting both accuracy and interpretability. To address these challenges, we propose a Series Saliency (SS) module that effectively perceives key trend information during both training and interpretation processes while exploring the previously uncharted sample space. In the training process, we leverage a Large Language Model (LLM) to guide the SS module in adaptively incorporating trend information to improve generalization. While in the interpretation process, we update the SS module to identify trend information for prediction and leverage the LLM’s domain knowledge to provide intuitive natural language explanations. We conduct comprehensive experiments from qualitative and quantitative perspectives to demonstrate the SS module’s superiority and plug-in benefits. Our code is included in the supplementary materials for examination and will be published upon acceptance.

title: On Kernel Eigen-Alignments of KRR: Reconstruction and Generalization
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the critical role of Eigenalignments between the kernel matrix and learning targets in achieving robust generalization in learning problems. We establish a direct connection between generalization performance in kernel methods and the estimation of Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues of matrices, offering a more intuitive understanding compared to prior work with minimal assumptions. We also show that, since the prediction task in KRR is essentially the weighted sum of Eigenvectors/singular vectors, by analyzing how much error can be caused by perturbations to the kernel matrix, we can then derive a bound on this generalization error using the estimation stability of matrix Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors. Compared with previous work, our analysis concentrates on finite-sample settings and on the generalization error arising from having a suboptimal finite training set. Our findings reveal that in kernel methods, as long as the kernel is of high rank, the near-zero reconstruction error can be trivially obtained, implying that the reconstruction error will have limited predictive power for generalization. Additionally, we establish a generalization bound from an Eigenvalues/Eigenvectors estimation perspective, showing that strong generalization requires increasing Eigenvector alignment, Eigenvalue magnitude, or gaps between consecutive Eigenvalues. Finally, we also demonstrate empirically our simplified risk estimator is able to track testing errors in trailing Eigendirections more closely than the existing literature.

title: SURGE: Structural Perturbation Response Field Guided Residual Distillation for Graph Unlearning
abstract: We introduce SURGE, a graph unlearning framework that treats deletion requests as prediction-level structural perturbations. Graph unlearning requires removing requested nodes, edges, or features from a trained graph neural network (GNN) without full retraining while preserving utility on retained data. Existing approaches either disrupt graph structure through partitioning, approximate removal in parameter space, or rely on fixed neighborhoods that cannot express heterogeneous node sensitivity. SURGE addresses this limitation with a Sense–Repair–Distill pipeline: it estimates a continuous response field over all nodes, solves graph-regularized corrected logits without backpropagation, and transfers the corrected knowledge through response-adaptive distillation. Across seven standard benchmarks and multiple GNN backbones, SURGE achieves leading or competitive utility and forgetting effectiveness for node, edge, and feature unlearning. In a matched 18-cell evaluation across deletion types, datasets, backbones, and ten random seeds, SURGE attains the highest mean micro-F1 (0.8632) and retraining faithfulness (0.0243 test JSD) among SURGE, ETR, MEGU, and IDEA; an ogbn-arxiv ablation further supports scalability on a large graph.

title: Beyond Lipschitz: generalization and optimization analysis for adversarial training under Hölder-type conditions
abstract: Adversarial training improves model robustness but may exhibit robust overfitting. Previous theoretical analyses mostly emphasize Lipschitz continuity of the adversarial loss, while understanding under weaker smoothness conditions (often observed in practice) remains limited. This paper investigates this problem in adversarial training, focusing on the generalization and optimization analyses of adversarial losses under weaker smoothness. We introduce Hölder continuity for the adversarial loss and propose a new concept of approximate Hölder smoothness, extending classical analyses from Lipschitz assumptions to a more general regime. A stability analysis for adversarial training is then developed, forming the theoretical basis for analyzing generalization and optimization. Under these conditions, we establish upper bounds on the generalization error and optimization gap of stochastic gradient descent for both convex and non-convex adversarial losses, and analyze the induced excess risk. These findings apply to a broad class of non-Lipschitz but Hölder smooth losses in deep learning, and offer theoretical insights into how optimization and generalization interact in adversarial training, contributing to a systematic understanding of robust overfitting. Furthermore, we empirically validate our theoretical findings using a practical example, demonstrating that the framework accurately captures generalization behavior under adversarial training.

title: TACCO: Actor–Critic Contrastive Optimization for OOD Action Mitigation in Offline Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning provides a viable solution for tasks where online interaction is costly or infeasible by leveraging pre-collected data for policy learning. However, in an offline setting, the policy improvement process is prone to value overestimation due to distribution shifts, which can lead to policy degradation. Existing methods primarily address this issue through policy constraints or conservative value regularization, but few explicitly model the problem actions from a representation learning perspective. This paper proposes TACCO (TD3+BC with Actor-Critic Contrastive Optimization), a contrastive offline reinforcement learning method based on the TD3+BC framework, designed to address the out-of-distribution (OOD) action problem in offline reinforcement learning. We define OOD actions as those that lack local data support in a given state, do not match the current state, or exhibit low reliability. Furthermore, for dense and sparse reward environments, we design two distinct contrastive learning policies: TACCO-A performs contrastive learning on the actor side between data-driven actions, random actions, and cross-state policy actions; TACCO-B filters reliable samples on the critic side based on high Q-values and low uncertainty, and applies contrastive constraints to both reliable and remaining samples simultaneously. In this paper, we compare TACCO with six state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning algorithms on the Mujoco and Adroit environments within the D4RL benchmark. Experimental results demonstrate that TACCO achieves superior performance on most tasks, validating its effectiveness in mitigating OOD action interference and enhancing policy stability.

title: Grid-based Decision Tree Learning
abstract: Decision tree learning algorithms, such as Classification and Regression Trees (CART), are commonly founded on heuristics that greedily maximize purity gain. Despite their practical success, the theoretical properties of these algorithms, such as consistency, remain unclear. This paper uncovers a substantial obstacle in analyzing the consistency of decision tree learning algorithms, in which the worst-case purity gain can be zero and a gain value of zero usually results in a non-convergent training error. Building upon this observation, our previous work introduced GridCART, a grid-based decision tree that can yield positive purity gain and achieve consistency under Lipschitz smoothness and a product feature distribution. This article extends the grid-based construction to random forests and gradient boosting decision trees, and establishes consistency-rate upper bounds for Grid-based Random Forests (GridForest) and a square-loss specialization of the Grid-based Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GridGBDT). Experiments on 20 OpenML datasets show that the grid-based ensembles perform comparably to their conventional counterparts.

title: A Survey on Loss-based Regularization for Model Generalization
abstract: Regularization is a central and fundamental research topic in machine learning. Despite the numerous methods developed in current fast growing literature, there is a lack of theoretical understanding and rigorous analysis of regularization. The first part of this paper is an answer to this need: we formulate regularization as a solution of ill-posed problems, examine fundamental principles of regularization, analyze the effectiveness of Tikhonov regularization in linear systems, and propose a consistency principle for the design of regularization methods in both linear and nonlinear systems. Based on these analyses, the second part of this paper is a survey of recent loss-based regularizers. We develop a comprehensive taxonomy and summarize prominent features of these regularizers. Finally, results of benchmark tests confirm the effectiveness of representative loss-based regularizers.

title: KARAMEL: Knowledge-Aware Ranking for Multimodal Entity Linking in the Arts via Heterogeneous Graphs
abstract: Discovering and disambiguating entities from multimodal and heterogeneous data is a key challenge in discovery science, where relevant knowledge is often implicit and distributed across modalities. We present KARAMEL, a framework for multimodal entity linking (MEL)—the task of aligning visual and textual mentions to entities in a knowledge base—in the cultural heritage domain. Unlike prior vision–language models that primarily rely on surface-level multimodal alignment, our approach incorporates sociohistorical and contextual knowledge through a knowledge-aware architecture that fuses a vision–language encoder with a heterogeneous graph neural network. This design enables contextual reasoning over complex relational structures and supports robust entity disambiguation under ambiguous or underspecified evidence. To benchmark multimodal discovery in this setting, we introduce \(\mathcal {W}\) iki \(\mathcal {M}\) u \(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{A}\) ( \(\mathcal {W}\) ikidata-based \(\mathcal {M}\) ultimodal \(\mathcal {S}\) emantic data for \(\mathcal {A}\) rt), a new dataset that links artworks to Wikidata entities via images, textual descriptions, and structured contextual knowledge. Experimental results on both \(\mathcal {W}\) iki \(\mathcal {M}\) u \(\mathcal{S}\mathcal{A}\) and MELArt show that KARAMEL surpasses strong baselines, particularly on implicit or abstract mentions, while ablation studies highlight the critical role of domain-specific, structured context in learning expressive representations. These results suggest that KARAMEL has potential for other scientific applications where knowledge is critical for better entity linking. Both the dataset and the code are publicly available on Zenodo ( https://zenodo.org/records/23019880 ) and GitHub ( https://github.com/cilabuniba/karamel ).

title: MMT: Achieving Exact Federated Unlearning with Improved Post-unlearning Performance
abstract: Federated learning allows multiple clients to collaboratively train a shared global model by sharing only model updates, such as gradients or parameters, to a central server without sharing their private data. Even though the clients do not share their private data, their shared model updates across multiple communication rounds indirectly influence the global model. This indirect influence poses significant challenges in many real-life applications, where it is necessary to completely remove a specific client’s influence (exact unlearning) from the global model. For example, exact unlearning may be required to comply with privacy regulations such as the GDPR’s Right to be Forgotten, or to remove the influence of malicious or poisoned clients in security-sensitive applications (e.g., jointly trained fraud detection models), where eliminating their influence is necessary to maintain the model’s performance. While retraining the global model with the remaining clients from scratch can achieve exact unlearning, it inevitably introduces significant deployment delays and leads to severe performance degradation due to random initialization, making it impractical for time-sensitive applications. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes two exact federated unlearning algorithms, Bi-Models Training ( bmt ) and Multi-Models Training ( mmt ), that ensure immediate exact unlearning by design while achieving better performance post-unlearning. bmt preserves isolated local model copies during training and uses them to provide a stronger initialization for the global FL model after unlearning. To capture the joint influence of multiple clients, mmt trains a carefully constructed set of sub-FL models on disjoint client subsets to avoid overlapping influence, and then aggregates the most influential unaffected models to reinitialize the global FL model. Our experiments on vision and language tasks demonstrate that bmt consistently outperforms existing exact unlearning baselines, while mmt achieves over \(2\times\) improvement in post-unlearning performance, all while maintaining exact unlearning guarantees and compatibility with arbitrary federated learning protocols.

title: RLAX: A Reinforcement Learning-Based Framework for Explaining Anomalous Data
abstract: Abstract Singling out the most informative features able to discriminate between normal and anomalous data is a formidable problem dealing with the enormous search space represented by the power set of the whole feature set. These features indeed encode the explanation of the deviating behavior associated with selected observations and represent the hidden knowledge of interest for the analyst in many applicative contexts, namely cybersecurity, bioinformatics, and green by AI, to cite a few. In this work, we present RLAX, a reinforcement learning-based algorithm detecting explanations from collections of high-dimensional data sets. The algorithm receives in input the unlabelled data collection of normal instances, a small set of labelled inlier examples, and a small set of anomalies to be explained. Separation between normal samples and anomalies is measured by means of a distance-based outlier score. The designed learning strategy thus induces a ranking among features that allows isolating those maximizing separation accuracy. Beyond an add-only formulation, we investigate a subspace refinement strategy that augments the action space with remove and stop actions, enabling non-monotone refinement and adaptive early termination. Experimental results highlight that the size of the explanation returned consists of a small fraction of the whole feature set, and that the associated accuracy and subspace margin are of remarkable quality. Additional analyses of the refinement strategy further clarify its impact on exploration efficiency and explanation quality.

title: Addressing Methodological Challenges in Time Series Anomaly Detection
abstract: Abstract Time series anomaly detection focuses on detecting unexpected events in time series data. Traditional techniques for this task include SVMs, k -Nearest Neighbors and PCA, while more recent approaches frequently employ deep learning, e.g., using variational autoencoders and graph neural networks. In several studies, these more elaborate techniques are regularly found to outperform traditional approaches. We present an in-depth review of 18 influential papers on time series anomaly detection using deep learning and found recurring methodological issues which lead to questionable or inconclusive results; leakage, modified datasets, and unclear baselines. We illustrate the importance of these issues with a novel empirical investigation and demonstrate it is not trivial to replicate reported relative performance of classical and deep learning methods. We find that older methods are frequently shown to perform worse than our non optimized implementations. We fail to reject the assumption of similar performance between these older and state of the art deep learning approaches on standard benchmark datasets.

title: Product Manifold Flow Matching for Mixed-Type Tabular Data Generation
abstract: Synthetic tabular data generation is increasingly important for privacy-preserving machine learning in healthcare, finance, and other regulated industries. Many current methods embed categorical variables into continuous spaces, which can blur their discrete structure and introduce interpolations between categorical states. Here, we propose flow matching on product manifolds, where each variable type resides on its natural geometric space: continuous variables in Euclidean space, categorical variables on probability simplexes with Fisher-Rao geometry, and ordinal variables on order-preserving arcs of unit circles. Our framework employs coordinate-wise vector field decomposition for manifold-specific processing and geometry-aware midpoint aggregation to capture inter-type dependencies with preserved geometric consistency. We evaluate the method on 12 benchmark datasets that range from small clinical records to educational datasets with over 101 million samples. Results show measurable improvements in generation quality, particularly on categorical-heavy and large-scale datasets. Geometric constraints also exhibit empirical resistance to memorization without explicit noise injection, as measured by distance to the closest record and membership inference metrics. The coordinate-wise structure enables efficient parallel computation that scales well to large datasets.

title: The Challenges of Hyperparameter Tuning for Accurate Causal Effect Estimation
abstract: Abstract ML is playing an increasingly crucial role in estimating causal effects of treatments on outcomes from observational data. Many ML methods (‘causal estimators’) have been proposed for this task. All of these methods, as with any ML approach, require extensive hyperparameter tuning. For non-causal predictive tasks, there is a consensus on the choice of tuning metrics (e.g. mean squared error), making it simple to compare models. However, for causal inference tasks, such a consensus is yet to be reached, making a any comparison of causal models difficult. On top of that, there is no ideal metric on which to tune causal estimators, so one must rely on proxies. Furthermore, the fact that model selection in causal inference involves multiple components (causal estimator, ML regressor, hyperparameters, metric), complicates the issue even further. In order to evaluate the importance of each component, we perform an extensive empirical study on their combination. Our experimental setup involves many commonly used causal estimators, regressors (‘base learners’ henceforth) and metrics applied to four well-known causal inference benchmark datasets. Our results show that hyperparameter tuning increased the probability of reaching state-of-the-art performance in average ( $$65\% {\rightarrow } 81\%$$ ) and individualised ( $$50\% {\rightarrow } 57\%$$ ) effect estimation with only commonly used estimators. We also show that the performance of standard metrics can be inconsistent across different scenarios. Our findings highlight the need for further research to establish whether metrics uniformly capable of state-of-the-art performance in causal model evaluation can be found.

title: Beyond Likelihood Ratio Bias: Nested Multi-time Scale Stochastic Approximation for Likelihood-Free Parameter Estimation
abstract: We study parameter inference in simulation-based stochastic models where the analytical form of the likelihood is unknown. The main difficulty is that score evaluation as a ratio of noisy Monte Carlo estimators induces bias and instability, which we overcome with a ratio-free nested multi-time-scale (NMTS) stochastic approximation (SA) method that simultaneously tracks the score and drives the parameter update. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the proposed NMTS algorithm for solving likelihood-free inference problems, including strong convergence, asymptotic normality, and convergence rates. We show that our algorithm can eliminate the original asymptotic bias \(O\big (\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}}\big )\) and accelerate the convergence rate from \(O\big (\beta _k+\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}}\big )\) to \(O\big (\frac{\beta _k}{\alpha _k}+\sqrt{\frac{\alpha _k}{N}}\big )\) , where N is the fixed batch size, \(\alpha _k\) and \(\beta _k\) are decreasing step sizes with \(\alpha _k\) , \(\beta _k\) , \(\beta _k/\alpha _k\rightarrow 0\) . With proper choice of \(\alpha _k\) and \(\beta _k\) , our convergence rates can match the optimal rate in the multi-time-scale SA literature. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our algorithm can improve the estimation accuracy by one to two orders of magnitude at the same computational cost, making it efficient for parameter estimation in stochastic systems.

title: Weighted UnLearning from Experience for Improved Spurious Correlation Robustness
abstract: Abstract Despite their success, Deep Learning (DL) models are susceptible to spurious correlations. These are accidental correlations between non-predictive features of the training dataset and the target label, leading to models that do not generalise well to samples without such spurious correlations. We propose to address this failure mode by extending and improving an existing method for spurious correlation robustness — UnLearning from Experience (ULE). ULE trains two models in parallel; a biased model is encouraged to learn the spurious correlations, while a separate debiased model is trained to solve the same task while avoiding learning the same behaviour as the first, thus avoiding learning the spurious correlations. A weakness of ULE is that it treats every training example identically, regardless of whether or not it contains a spurious correlation. Therefore, ULE does not make optimal use of the training data, leading to worse-than-necessary performance. To address this weakness, we introduce Weighted UnLearning from Experience (wULE), which modifies the original ULE loss function to reweight the components depending on whether a training sample likely contains spurious correlations. Hence, we explore two methods for identifying training samples likely to contain spurious correlations. We test our approach using several well-known spurious correlation robustness benchmarks — Waterbirds, CelebA, UrbanCars and MultiNLI. Our novel wULE method outperforms the original ULE in all cases and achieves Worst-Group Accuracy (WGA) results comparable to the best methods in the spurious correlation robustness literature.

title: Optimizing AlphaPose with Dual Non-Local Attention for Real-Time Unsafe Behavior Detection in Mining Environments
abstract: In the mining industry, unsafe worker behaviors pose significant safety risks. Recent advances in deep learning have improved unsafe behavior recognition; however, challenges remain in achieving both real-time performance and high accuracy under complex mining conditions, as well as in the availability of dedicated datasets. To address these issues, we introduce a comprehensive miner unsafe behavior dataset and propose the Mining Industry Unsafe Behaviors Monitoring Framework (MIUBM-Net), which integrates STFNet-A for typical unsafe behavior detection and Alpha-SDL-Pose, based on Dual Non-Local Attention (DNLA), for posture-related unsafe behavior recognition. STFNet-A achieves 96.9% mAP at 59.6 FPS, while Alpha-SDL-Pose improves posture recognition accuracy to 94.9% at 49.4 FPS. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and its constituent modules for recognizing typical and posture-related unsafe behaviors in underground mining environments, providing a practical solution for intelligent mining safety monitoring.

title: FedXAI: Federated Medical Imaging with Intrinsic Explainability and Differentially Private Explanation Auditing
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative medical imaging training without sharing raw data. However, existing frameworks treat privacy, interpretability, and cross-site explanation consistency as separate objectives. We present FedXAI , a unified framework that substantially mitigates this trilemma within a single architecture. FedXAI introduces three components: (i) Self-Explainable Federated Architecture (SEFA), which integrates an EfficientNet-B0 backbone with a 32-dimensional hybrid concept-bottleneck layer anchored to RadLex radiological ontology terms; (ii) Federated Explanation Aggregation Protocol (FEAP), which extends server-side aggregation with a cosine-consistency penalty to align client explanation spaces; and (iii) the Privacy-Preserving Explanation Verification (PPEV) module, which audits cross-client explanation quality via the subsampled Gaussian mechanism with Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) accounting. Evaluated on the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset with non-IID Dirichlet partitioning ( \(\alpha = 0.5\) ) across five simulated hospital clients, FedXAI achieves a mean AUC of 0.7349, outperforming FedAvg (0.7193), FedProx (0.7241), SCAFFOLD (0.7268), FedBN (0.7285), and MOON (0.7301). Simultaneously, it increases cross-client explanation consistency from 83.6% to 99.9%. The PPEV module provides formal \((\varepsilon ,\delta )\) -differential privacy for the explanation-audit channel, certifying \(\varepsilon = 0.1394\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) . Model parameter transmission follows the standard FL architectural separation, while end-to-end DP-SGD training is left for future work. On the benchmark studied here, FedXAI demonstrates that privacy, diagnostic accuracy, and interpretability in federated medical imaging can be advanced simultaneously through principled architectural integration.
